title: the Sama Veda as song
hook: na na na, hey hey. songs everywhere carry syllables that mean nothing. the Sama Veda's chants have them too, and the Chandogya gives them a world

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sama Veda as song, and the gods' search for what could carry the high chant: every sense went both ways, and the main breath held.

Na na na na. Hey hey. Ooh, la la. Plenty of songs have a stretch where the words run out and the singer keeps going anyway. Nobody looks those syllables up. And yet a crowd of strangers will sing them back, louder than the verses. Sama Veda chant has syllables like that too, sounds slipped between the words of the verse to carry the melody. A reader could skip them as filler. The Chandogya Upanishad doesn't. Today: the sounds between the words.
screen: `NA NA NA. HEY HEY.` → `NOT IN ANY DICTIONARY.` → `THE SOUNDS BETWEEN THE WORDS.`

segments.voice: When a verse becomes a saman, a Sama Veda chant, the words don't stay as they were. Vowels stretch. Syllables repeat. And between them come extra sounds, with names like hau and hai and auhoyi. These are stobhas. On their own they don't mean anything the way a word does; they're there for the song. Then the Chandogya gives the stobhas the world. In paraphrase: this world is the sound hau. The wind is hai. The moon is atha. And it goes on down a list, pairing chant-sounds with fire, with the sun, with breath, with food. So the sounds a hurried listener would call filler, the Upanishad treats as the places where the whole world comes into the song: earth, wind, moon, riding in syllables with no dictionary meaning. Readers take this more than one way. Some hear a meditation, a way for the singer to hold the whole world in mind while chanting. Some hear a deeper point about sound: meaning isn't only in what a word says, but in what a sound can hold. The Chandogya doesn't settle it. It just refuses to throw the small sounds away. And ordinary days are full of stobhas: the hmm while a friend talks, the oh when someone hands you coffee, the sigh at the end of a long day. Nothing in a dictionary. Not nothing.
screen: `STRETCHED, REPEATED, FILLED IN.` · `STOBHAS: HAU, HAI, AUHOYI.` · `THIS WORLD IS HAU. THE WIND IS HAI.` · `THE SMALL SOUNDS ARE NOT THROWN AWAY.`

segments.voice: On the out-breath let a soft open sound come, like haa or hau, quiet enough that no one else hears, just a sound with no meaning. On the next breaths make the same sound and let it hold one thing each time, the ground under you, the air in the room; if silence suits the place you're in, make the sound inside. If you pray, let it be prayer.
The Sama Veda as song. In the chant, small sounds called stobhas carry the melody, and the Chandogya pairs them with the world. Today's word.
screen: `THE SAMA VEDA AS SONG — today's word`.

chat.says: Are those hau and hai sounds in Sama Veda chant just filler?
options: Not to the Chandogya: it pairs them with the world, hau this world, hai the wind.
Yes, the Chandogya says to drop them so the real words come through clearly.
No, each one is a short word with a dictionary meaning, like a name.
chat.meaning: Stobhas carry the melody without word meaning, and Chandogya 1.13 pairs them with the world: this world is hau, the wind hai, the moon atha.
